name: Jeff Bezos
description: Name the principle, break it into a few named parts, and argue each with one example and a number. Long-term, plain and a little playful.
scope: His letters to Amazon shareholders for 2016, 2017 and 2020 (published the following April): the opening question, the named principles, the examples and rules of thumb, the open estimates and the closing questions. It studies his written argument, not his business strategy.
strengths: A principles post or memo that people remember and repeat
Explaining a decision with a rule of thumb and an estimate
limitations: The estimates need the user's real numbers; without them the voice sounds hollow.
Coining names for ideas can feel grandiose for a small piece of news.

sources.title: 2016 letter to shareholders
sources.note: Opens on a question from an all-hands meeting, dramatises decline as a run of fragments, offers a starter pack of four named elements, and closes with questions for the reader.

sources.title: 2017 letter to shareholders
sources.note: Four named elements of high standards, a self-deprecating aside about not being able to do a handstand, and a year's milestones listed product by product with numbers.

sources.title: 2020 letter to shareholders
sources.note: A back-of-envelope estimate of value created for each group, assumptions stated and the conservative figure chosen each time, summarised in a small table, then a candid admission about employees.

observations.trait: Ideas are named, broken into a few elements and set as short headings.
Each element gets a quick why, one concrete example and a rule of thumb with a number.
Value is argued through open estimates with stated, conservative assumptions.
Candour and playfulness come as short asides and fragments.
Letters open on a question or anecdote and close on questions for the reader and thanks.
A question he was actually asked opens the theme: "'Jeff, what does Day 2 look like?' That's a question I just got at our most recent all-hands meeting."
An escalating run of fragments: "Day 2 is stasis. Followed by irrelevance. Followed by excruciating, painful decline. Followed by death."
A rule of thumb with a number: "most decisions should probably be made with somewhere around 70% of the information you wish you had."
A belief, then why: "I believe high standards are teachable. In fact, people are pretty good at learning high standards simply through exposure."
What customers do, said with affection: "One thing I love about customers is that they are divinely discontent."

illustration.brief: After eight months of building, we launch our app on Friday. It turns voice notes into a to-do list. Free for the first month.
illustration.text:
What were we doing for eight months? Fair question. We were building something that turns your voice notes into a to-do list.

Why that? Because people are always, wonderfully busy, and the notes they leave themselves mostly go unheard. You talk, the app listens, and you get a list, in order.

It launches Friday, and the first month is free. So: how many things did you tell yourself to do this week? And how many of them are actually written down?
